claim: Kinetochores are macromolecular protein complexes at centromeres that ensure accurate chromosome segregation by attaching chromosomes to spindle microtubules and integrating safeguard mechanisms.
source: Kinetochores are macromolecular protein complexes at centromeres that ensure accurate chromosome segregation by attaching chromosomes to spindle microtubules and integrating safeguard mechanisms.
evidence: This is a general statement about kinetochore function that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The inner kinetochore is assembled on CENP-A nucleosomes.
source: The inner kinetochore is assembled on CENP-A nucleosomes and has been implicated in establishing a kinetochore-associated pool of Aurora B kinase, a chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) subunit, which is essential for chromosome biorientation.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about kinetochore assembly on CENP-A nucleosomes.

claim: The inner kinetochore has been implicated in establishing a kinetochore-associated pool of Aurora B kinase, a chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) subunit, which is essential for chromosome biorientation.
source: The inner kinetochore is assembled on CENP-A nucleosomes and has been implicated in establishing a kinetochore-associated pool of Aurora B kinase, a chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) subunit, which is essential for chromosome biorientation.
evidence: This statement references prior research findings about the role of the inner kinetochore in CPC localization.

claim: The Ame1/Okp1CENP-U/Q heterodimer, which forms the COMA complex with Ctf19/Mcm21CENP-P/O, selectively bound Cse4CENP-A nucleosomes through the Cse4 N-terminus.
source: By performing crosslink-guided in vitro reconstitution of budding yeast kinetochore complexes we showed that the Ame1/Okp1CENP-U/Q heterodimer, which forms the COMA complex with Ctf19/Mcm21CENP-P/O, selectively bound Cse4CENP-A nucleosomes through the Cse4 N-terminus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the in vitro reconstitution experiments and crosslinking data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Sli15/Ipl1INCENP/Aurora-B core-CPC interacted with COMA in vitro through the Ctf19 C-terminus.
source: The Sli15/Ipl1INCENP/Aurora-B core-CPC interacted with COMA in vitro through the Ctf19 C-terminus whose deletion affected chromosome segregation fidelity in Sli15 wild-type cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro binding assays and crosslinking data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Deletion of the Ctf19 C-terminus affected chromosome segregation fidelity in Sli15 wild-type cells.
source: The Sli15/Ipl1INCENP/Aurora-B core-CPC interacted with COMA in vitro through the Ctf19 C-terminus whose deletion affected chromosome segregation fidelity in Sli15 wild-type cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the minichromosome loss assay data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Tethering Sli15 to Ame1/Okp1 rescued synthetic lethality upon Ctf19 depletion in a Sli15 centromere-targeting deficient mutant.
source: Tethering Sli15 to Ame1/Okp1 rescued synthetic lethality upon Ctf19 depletion in a Sli15 centromere-targeting deficient mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast viability assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Kinetochore assembly is restricted to centromeres, chromosomal domains that are marked by the presence of the histone H3 variant Cse4CENP-A.
source: Kinetochore assembly is restricted to centromeres, chromosomal domains that are marked by the presence of the histone H3 variant Cse4CENP-A (human ortholog names are superscripted if appropriate) (Earnshaw and Rothfield, 1985; Fukagawa and Earnshaw, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Earnshaw and Rothfield, 1985; Fukagawa and Earnshaw, 2014).

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae has point centromeres, which are characterized by a specific ~125 bp DNA sequence wrapped around a single Cse4-containing histone octamer.
source: In contrast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae has point centromeres, which are characterized by a specific ~125 bp DNA sequence wrapped around a single Cse4-containing histone octamer (Fitzgerald-Hayes et al., 1982; Camahort et al., 2009; Hasson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Fitzgerald-Hayes et al., 1982; Camahort et al., 2009; Hasson et al., 2013).

claim: The budding yeast kinetochore is composed of about 45 core subunits which are organized in different stable complexes.
source: The budding yeast kinetochore is composed of about 45 core subunits which are organized in different stable complexes (De Wulf et al., 2003; Westermann et al., 2003) of which several are present in multiple copies (Joglekar et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (De Wulf et al., 2003; Westermann et al., 2003; Joglekar et al., 2006).

claim: Several kinetochore complexes are present in multiple copies.
source: The budding yeast kinetochore is composed of about 45 core subunits which are organized in different stable complexes (De Wulf et al., 2003; Westermann et al., 2003) of which several are present in multiple copies (Joglekar et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Joglekar et al., 2006).

claim: The kinetochore proteins are evolutionary largely conserved between yeast and humans.
source: The kinetochore proteins are evolutionary largely conserved between yeast and humans (Westermann and Schleiffer, 2013; van Hooff et al., 2017) and share a similar hierarchy of assembly from DNA to the microtubule binding interface (De Wulf et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Westermann and Schleiffer, 2013; van Hooff et al., 2017).

claim: Kinetochore proteins share a similar hierarchy of assembly from DNA to the microtubule binding interface.
source: The kinetochore proteins are evolutionary largely conserved between yeast and humans (Westermann and Schleiffer, 2013; van Hooff et al., 2017) and share a similar hierarchy of assembly from DNA to the microtubule binding interface (De Wulf et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (De Wulf et al., 2003).

claim: The CTF19c comprises the Chl4/Iml3CENP-N/L, Mcm16/Ctf3/Mcm22CENP-H/I/K, Cnn1/Wip1CENP-T/W, Mhf1/Mhf2CENP-S/X and Ctf19/Okp1/Mcm21/Ame1CENP-P/Q/O/U (COMA) complexes plus Mif2CENP-C.
source: The CTF19c comprises the Chl4/Iml3CENP-N/L, Mcm16/Ctf3/Mcm22CENP-H/I/K, Cnn1/Wip1CENP-T/W, Mhf1/Mhf2CENP-S/X and Ctf19/Okp1/Mcm21/Ame1CENP-P/Q/O/U (COMA) complexes plus Mif2CENP-C (Cheeseman et al., 2002; Westermann et al., 2003; Biggins, 2013; Musacchio and Desai, 2017) and the budding-yeast specific Nkp1/Nkp2 heterodimer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Cheeseman et al., 2002; Westermann et al., 2003; Biggins, 2013; Musacchio and Desai, 2017).

claim: The budding-yeast specific Nkp1/Nkp2 heterodimer is part of the CTF19c.
source: The CTF19c comprises the Chl4/Iml3CENP-N/L, Mcm16/Ctf3/Mcm22CENP-H/I/K, Cnn1/Wip1CENP-T/W, Mhf1/Mhf2CENP-S/X and Ctf19/Okp1/Mcm21/Ame1CENP-P/Q/O/U (COMA) complexes plus Mif2CENP-C (Cheeseman et al., 2002; Westermann et al., 2003; Biggins, 2013; Musacchio and Desai, 2017) and the budding-yeast specific Nkp1/Nkp2 heterodimer.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the composition of the budding yeast kinetochore.

claim: The CBF3 (Ndc10/Cep3/Ctf13/Skp1) complex has been identified as sequence-specific binder of the centromeric DNA sequence CDEIII.
source: Another yeast inner kinetochore complex, the CBF3 (Ndc10/Cep3/Ctf13/Skp1) complex, has been identified as sequence-specfic binder of the centromeric DNA sequence CDEIII (Ng and Carbon, 1987; Lechner and Carbon, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Ng and Carbon, 1987; Lechner and Carbon, 1991).

claim: The CTF19cCCAN provides a cooperative high-affinity binding environment for the Cse4CENP-A-NCP.
source: The CTF19cCCAN provides a cooperative high-affinity binding environment for the Cse4CENP-A-NCP (Weir et al., 2016), where distinct subunits selectively recognize Cse4CENP-A specific features.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Weir et al., 2016).

claim: Distinct CTF19cCCAN subunits selectively recognize Cse4CENP-A specific features.
source: The CTF19cCCAN provides a cooperative high-affinity binding environment for the Cse4CENP-A-NCP (Weir et al., 2016), where distinct subunits selectively recognize Cse4CENP-A specific features.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about CCAN-CENP-A interactions.

claim: Across different species the CENP-C signature motif interacts with divergent hydrophobic residues of the CENP-A C-terminal tail.
source: Across different species the CENP-C signature motif interacts with divergent hydrophobic residues of the CENP-A C-terminal tail (Musacchio and Desai, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Musacchio and Desai, 2017).

claim: Electron microscopy studies have recently resolved the interaction of CENP-N with the CENP-A centromere-targeting domain (CATD) in vertebrates.
source: Electron microscopy studies have recently resolved the interaction of CENP-N with the CENP-A centromere-targeting domain (CATD) in vertebrates (Carroll et al., 2009; Guse et al., 2011; Pentakota et al., 2017; Chittori et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Carroll et al., 2009; Guse et al., 2011; Pentakota et al., 2017; Chittori et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2018).

claim: For budding yeast Cse4, a direct interaction has so far only been demonstrated with Mif2.
source: For budding yeast Cse4, a direct interaction has so far only been demonstrated with Mif2 (Westermann et al., 2003; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Westermann et al., 2003; Xiao et al., 2017).

claim: Apart from Mif2, the only essential CTF19cCCAN proteins are Ame1 and Okp1.
source: Apart from Mif2, the only essential CTF19cCCAN proteins are Ame1 and Okp1 (Meluh and Koshland, 1997; Ortiz et al., 1999; De Wulf et al., 2003), with the N-terminus of Ame1 binding the N-terminal domain of Mtw1 and thus serving as docking site for the outer kinetochore KMN network (KNL1SPC105-/MIS12MTW1-/NDC80NDC80-complexes) (Hornung et al., 2014; Dimitrova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Meluh and Koshland, 1997; Ortiz et al., 1999; De Wulf et al., 2003).

claim: The N-terminus of Ame1 binds the N-terminal domain of Mtw1 and thus serves as docking site for the outer kinetochore KMN network.
source: Apart from Mif2, the only essential CTF19cCCAN proteins are Ame1 and Okp1 (Meluh and Koshland, 1997; Ortiz et al., 1999; De Wulf et al., 2003), with the N-terminus of Ame1 binding the N-terminal domain of Mtw1 and thus serving as docking site for the outer kinetochore KMN network (KNL1SPC105-/MIS12MTW1-/NDC80NDC80-complexes) (Hornung et al., 2014; Dimitrova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Hornung et al., 2014; Dimitrova et al., 2016).

claim: Ipl1Aurora B is a subunit of the evolutionary conserved tetrameric chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) which associates close to the centromere from G1 until anaphase.
source: A major effector of both regulatory feedback loops is the kinase Ipl1Aurora B, a subunit of the evolutionary conserved tetrameric chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) which associates close to the centromere from G1 until anaphase (Biggins and Murray, 2001; Widlund et al., 2006; Carmena et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Biggins and Murray, 2001; Widlund et al., 2006; Carmena et al., 2012).

claim: The kinase subunit Ipl1Aurora B binds to the C-terminal IN-box domain of the scaffold protein Sli15INCENP.
source: The kinase subunit Ipl1Aurora B binds to the C-terminal IN-box domain (Adams et al., 2000; Kaitna et al., 2000) of the scaffold protein Sli15INCENP, and Nbl1Borealin and Bir1Survivin form a three-helix bundle with the Sli15 N-terminus (Klein et al., 2006; Jeyaprakash et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Adams et al., 2000; Kaitna et al., 2000).

claim: Nbl1Borealin and Bir1Survivin form a three-helix bundle with the Sli15 N-terminus.
source: The kinase subunit Ipl1Aurora B binds to the C-terminal IN-box domain (Adams et al., 2000; Kaitna et al., 2000) of the scaffold protein Sli15INCENP, and Nbl1Borealin and Bir1Survivin form a three-helix bundle with the Sli15 N-terminus (Klein et al., 2006; Jeyaprakash et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Klein et al., 2006; Jeyaprakash et al., 2007).

claim: All known mechanisms for recruitment of the CPC to the yeast centromere rely on Bir1, which directly associates with Ndc10.
source: All known mechanisms for recruitment of the CPC to the yeast centromere rely on Bir1, which directly associates with Ndc10 (Cho and Harrison, 2011) and is recruited through Sgo1 to histone H2A phosphorylated at S121 by Bub1 which so far has only been established in fission yeast (Kawashima et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Cho and Harrison, 2011).

claim: Bir1 is recruited through Sgo1 to histone H2A phosphorylated at S121 by Bub1 which so far has only been established in fission yeast.
source: All known mechanisms for recruitment of the CPC to the yeast centromere rely on Bir1, which directly associates with Ndc10 (Cho and Harrison, 2011) and is recruited through Sgo1 to histone H2A phosphorylated at S121 by Bub1 which so far has only been established in fission yeast (Kawashima et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Kawashima et al., 2010).

claim: During early mitosis incorrect microtubule attachment states are resolved by Ipl1Aurora B which phosphorylates Ndc80 and Dam1 sites within the microtubule binding interface and thereby reduces their affinity towards microtubules.
source: During early mitosis incorrect microtubule attachment states are resolved by Ipl1Aurora B which phosphorylates Ndc80 and Dam1 sites within the microtubule binding interface and thereby reduces their affinity towards microtubules (Cheeseman et al., 2002; Miranda et al., 2005; Westermann et al., 2005; Cheeseman et al., 2006; DeLuca et al., 2006; Santaguida and Musacchio, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Cheeseman et al., 2002; Miranda et al., 2005; Westermann et al., 2005; Cheeseman et al., 2006; DeLuca et al., 2006; Santaguida and Musacchio, 2009).

claim: A Sli15 mutant lacking the centromere-targeting domain, Sli15∆N2-228 (Sli15∆N), suppressed the deletion phenotypes of Bir1, Nbl1, Bub1 and Sgo1 that mediate recruitment of the CPC to the centromere.
source: A recent study challenged this model by showing that a Sli15 mutant lacking the centromere-targeting domain, Sli15∆N2-228 (Sli15∆N), suppressed the deletion phenotypes of Bir1, Nbl1, Bub1 and Sgo1 that mediate recruitment of the CPC to the centromere (Campbell and Desai, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Campbell and Desai, 2013).

claim: In contrast to wild-type Sli15, which localized between sister kinetochore clusters, Sli15∆N showed weak localization overlapping with Nuf2 at kinetochores.
source: In contrast to wild-type Sli15, which localized between sister kinetochore clusters, Sli15∆N showed weak localization overlapping with Nuf2 at kinetochores (Campbell and Desai, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Campbell and Desai, 2013).

claim: Sli15∆N was indistinguishably viable from wild-type and displayed no significant chromosome segregation defects.
source: Apart from the altered localization, Sli15∆N was indistinguishably viable from wild-type and displayed no significant chromosome segregation defects (Campbell and Desai, 2013; Hengeveld et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Campbell and Desai, 2013; Hengeveld et al., 2017).

claim: A survivin mutant in chicken DT40 cells that failed to localize INCENP and Aurora B to centromeres from prophase to metaphase displayed normal growth kinetics.
source: Similarly, a survivin mutant in chicken DT40 cells that failed to localize INCENP and Aurora B to centromeres from prophase to metaphase displayed normal growth kinetics (Yue et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Yue et al., 2008).

claim: Centromere-targeting of Sli15/Ipl1 is largely dispensable for error correction and SAC signaling.
source: These findings suggest that centromere-targeting of Sli15/Ipl1 is largely dispensable for error correction and SAC signaling.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings about Sli15∆N and survivin mutants mentioned in the preceding sentences.

claim: Subunits of the COMA complex were previously implicated in CPC function at kinetochores.
source: Subunits of the COMA complex were previously implicated in CPC function at kinetochores (De Wulf et al., 2003; Knockleby and Vogel, 2009) and the Sli15ΔN mutant showed synthetic lethality with deletions of Ctf19 or Mcm21 (Campbell and Desai, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (De Wulf et al., 2003; Knockleby and Vogel, 2009).

claim: The Sli15ΔN mutant showed synthetic lethality with deletions of Ctf19 or Mcm21.
source: Subunits of the COMA complex were previously implicated in CPC function at kinetochores (De Wulf et al., 2003; Knockleby and Vogel, 2009) and the Sli15ΔN mutant showed synthetic lethality with deletions of Ctf19 or Mcm21 (Campbell and Desai, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Campbell and Desai, 2013).

claim: Mif2 selectively interacted with Cse4-NCPs and not with H3-NCPs.
source: Consistent with a recent study (Xiao et al., 2017), using electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), we observed that Mif2 selectively interacted with Cse4-NCPs and not with H3-NCPs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 1A and is consistent with a cited study (Xiao et al., 2017).

claim: Ame1/Okp1 bound specifically to Cse4-NCPs.
source: We also found that Ame1/Okp1 bound specifically to Cse4-NCPs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The lack of interaction with H3-NCPs suggests that Ame1/Okp1 directly and selectively binds Cse4 and that the interaction does not require AT-rich DNA sequences as previously proposed.
source: The lack of interaction with H3-NCPs, which were reconstituted using the same 601 DNA sequence (Tachiwana et al., 2011), suggests that Ame1/Okp1 directly and selectively binds Cse4 and that the interaction does not require AT-rich DNA sequences as previously proposed (Hornung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Ame1/Okp1 binds Cse4-NCPs but not H3-NCPs reconstituted on the same DNA sequence, contradicting a previous proposal (Hornung et al., 2014).

claim: Chl4/Iml3 did not form distinct complexes with either Cse4- or H3-NCPs in the EMSA.
source: In contrast to the EMSA titration of human CCAN complexes with CENP-A-NCP (Weir et al., 2016) using 10 nM NCP mixed with up to 20-fold excess of the respective subcomplexes, we could not detect Cse4-NCP band shifts with Chl4/Iml3, the orthologs of human CENP-NL, and with Mcm16/Ctf3/Mcm22, the orthologs of human CENP-HIK (no S. cerevisiae ortholog of CENP-M has been identified) using 500 nM NCP incubated with a twofold excess of the complexes.
evidence: This claim is based on the EMSA data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Mcm16/Ctf3/Mcm22 did not form distinct complexes with either Cse4- or H3-NCPs in the EMSA.
source: In contrast to the EMSA titration of human CCAN complexes with CENP-A-NCP (Weir et al., 2016) using 10 nM NCP mixed with up to 20-fold excess of the respective subcomplexes, we could not detect Cse4-NCP band shifts with Chl4/Iml3, the orthologs of human CENP-NL, and with Mcm16/Ctf3/Mcm22, the orthologs of human CENP-HIK (no S. cerevisiae ortholog of CENP-M has been identified) using 500 nM NCP incubated with a twofold excess of the complexes.
evidence: This claim is based on the EMSA data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Ctf19/Mcm21, Cnn1/Wip1, Nkp1/Nkp2 and Mhf1/Mhf2 did not form distinct complexes with either Cse4- or H3-NCPs in the EMSA.
source: Ctf19/Mcm21, Cnn1/Wip1, Nkp1/Nkp2 and Mhf1/Mhf2 did also not form distinct complexes with either Cse4- or H3-NCPs in the EMSA indicating that Mif2 and Ame1/Okp1 possess a higher relative binding affinity to Cse4-NCPs than the other CTF19c subcomplexes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on the EMSA data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Mif2 and Ame1/Okp1 possess a higher relative binding affinity to Cse4-NCPs than the other CTF19c subcomplexes.
source: Ctf19/Mcm21, Cnn1/Wip1, Nkp1/Nkp2 and Mhf1/Mhf2 did also not form distinct complexes with either Cse4- or H3-NCPs in the EMSA indicating that Mif2 and Ame1/Okp1 possess a higher relative binding affinity to Cse4-NCPs than the other CTF19c subcomplexes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the EMSA data showing that only Mif2 and Ame1/Okp1 formed distinct complexes with Cse4-NCPs.

claim: In total 349 inter-subunit crosslinks between the fifteen proteins were identified in the Cse4-NCP:Mif2:COMA:Chl4/Iml3:MTW1c complex.
source: In total 349 inter-subunit crosslinks between the fifteen proteins were identified (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the XLMS data presented in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The majority of the crosslinks detected within the different subcomplexes MTW1c, COMA, Chl4/Iml3, and Cse4-NCP are in agreement with previous studies.
source: The majority of the crosslinks detected within the different subcomplexes MTW1c, COMA, Chl4/Iml3, and Cse4-NCP are in agreement with previous studies validating our crosslink map (De Wulf et al., 2003; Hinshaw and Harrison, 2013; Hornung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior research (De Wulf et al., 2003; Hinshaw and Harrison, 2013; Hornung et al., 2014).

claim: Crosslinks from the Mif2 N-terminus to the MTW1c are consistent with previously described interfaces.
source: Moreover, crosslinks from the Mif2 N-terminus to the MTW1c (Przewloka et al., 2011; Screpanti et al., 2011), from the Mif2 Chl4/Iml3-binding domain to Chl4 (Hinshaw and Harrison, 2013), and from the Mif2 signature motif to the Cse4 C-terminus (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1) (Kato et al., 2013) are consistent with previously described interfaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior research (Przewloka et al., 2011; Screpanti et al., 2011).

claim: Crosslinks from the Mif2 Chl4/Iml3-binding domain to Chl4 are consistent with previously described interfaces.
source: Moreover, crosslinks from the Mif2 N-terminus to the MTW1c (Przewloka et al., 2011; Screpanti et al., 2011), from the Mif2 Chl4/Iml3-binding domain to Chl4 (Hinshaw and Harrison, 2013), and from the Mif2 signature motif to the Cse4 C-terminus (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1) (Kato et al., 2013) are consistent with previously described interfaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior research (Hinshaw and Harrison, 2013).

claim: Crosslinks from the Mif2 signature motif to the Cse4 C-terminus are consistent with previously described interfaces.
source: Moreover, crosslinks from the Mif2 N-terminus to the MTW1c (Przewloka et al., 2011; Screpanti et al., 2011), from the Mif2 Chl4/Iml3-binding domain to Chl4 (Hinshaw and Harrison, 2013), and from the Mif2 signature motif to the Cse4 C-terminus (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1) (Kato et al., 2013) are consistent with previously described interfaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior research (Kato et al., 2013).

claim: Crosslinks between Ame1/Okp1 and Cse4 occur exclusively between Okp1 and Cse4.
source: Crosslinks between Ame1/Okp1 and Cse4 occur exclusively between Okp1 and Cse4, suggesting that Okp1 is the direct binding partner of Cse4.
evidence: This claim is based on the XLMS data presented in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Okp1 is the direct binding partner of Cse4.
source: Crosslinks between Ame1/Okp1 and Cse4 occur exclusively between Okp1 and Cse4, suggesting that Okp1 is the direct binding partner of Cse4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that crosslinks between Ame1/Okp1 and Cse4 occur exclusively between Okp1 and Cse4.

claim: Okp1 was the only COMA subunit that crosslinked to the three canonical histones H2A, H2B and H4 with the exception of one crosslink between Ame1 and H2A.
source: Furthermore, Okp1 was the only COMA subunit that crosslinked to the three canonical histones H2A, H2B and H4 with the exception of one crosslink between Ame1 and H2A.
evidence: This claim is based on the XLMS data presented in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: A direct interaction between COMA and Chl4 was reported previously.
source: Our analysis indicated a close association between Chl4/Iml3 and all COMA subunits. A direct interaction between COMA and Chl4 was reported previously and the Ctf19/Mcm21 heterodimer was found to be required for the kinetochore localization of Chl4 and Iml3 (Schmitzberger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Schmitzberger et al., 2017).

claim: The Ctf19/Mcm21 heterodimer was found to be required for the kinetochore localization of Chl4 and Iml3.
source: Our analysis indicated a close association between Chl4/Iml3 and all COMA subunits. A direct interaction between COMA and Chl4 was reported previously and the Ctf19/Mcm21 heterodimer was found to be required for the kinetochore localization of Chl4 and Iml3 (Schmitzberger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Schmitzberger et al., 2017).

claim: Two crosslinks were detected between Okp1 and the essential Cse4 N-terminus.
source: Two crosslinks were detected between Okp1 and the essential Cse4 N-terminus (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the XLMS data presented in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: A multiple sequence alignment of Cse4CENP-A protein sequences detected a conserved region (ScCse4 aa 34–61), unique to Cse4 proteins of interrelated yeasts.
source: A multiple sequence alignment (MSA) of Cse4CENP-A protein sequences (Figure 2A) detected a conserved region (ScCse4 aa 34–61), unique to Cse4 proteins of interrelated yeasts, which is almost identical to the so-called 'essential N-terminal domain' (END), aa 28–60, shown to be required for the essential function of the Cse4 N-terminus and for recruiting the 'Mcm21p/Ctf19p/Okp1p complex' to minichromosomes (Keith et al., 1999; Ortiz et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is based on the MSA shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The conserved region (ScCse4 aa 34–61) is almost identical to the so-called 'essential N-terminal domain' (END), aa 28–60, shown to be required for the essential function of the Cse4 N-terminus and for recruiting the 'Mcm21p/Ctf19p/Okp1p complex' to minichromosomes.
source: A multiple sequence alignment (MSA) of Cse4CENP-A protein sequences (Figure 2A) detected a conserved region (ScCse4 aa 34–61), unique to Cse4 proteins of interrelated yeasts, which is almost identical to the so-called 'essential N-terminal domain' (END), aa 28–60, shown to be required for the essential function of the Cse4 N-terminus and for recruiting the 'Mcm21p/Ctf19p/Okp1p complex' to minichromosomes (Keith et al., 1999; Ortiz et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Keith et al., 1999; Ortiz et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2000).

claim: Wild-type Cse4-NCP but not H3-NCP formed a stoichiometric complex with Ame1/Okp1.
source: Wild-type Cse4-NCP but not H3-NCP formed a stoichiometric complex with Ame1/Okp1 (Figure 2C) which is consistent with our EMSA and XLMS analyses (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 2C and is consistent with EMSA and XLMS data in Figure 1A,C.

claim: Ame1/Okp1 bound to a Cse4-NCP retained the ability to interact with the MTW1c.

claim: Cse4∆48–61 associated with Ame1/Okp1.

claim: Deletion of amino acids 34–46 completely disrupted the interaction between Cse4 and Ame1/Okp1.
source: To further narrow down the interface, two deletion mutants splitting the END in half, Cse4∆34–46 and Cse4∆48–61 (Figure 2B), were tested in SEC experiments. While Cse4∆48–61 associated with Ame1/Okp1, deletion of amino acids 34–46 completely disrupted the interaction (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The Cse4Δ48–61 mutant displayed wild-type growth rates.
source: To test whether this motif is essential for cell viability, we depleted endogenous Cse4 from the nucleus using the anchor-away technique and performed rescue experiments by ectopically expressing the Cse4 mutants Cse4∆34–46 and Cse4∆48–61. Indeed, deletion of amino acids 34–46 was lethal, whereas the Cse4Δ48–61 mutant displayed wild-type growth rates (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast viability assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The observation that deletion of the minimal Ame1/Okp1 interacting Cse4 motif (aa 34–46) correlates with the loss of cell viability suggests that binding of the Ame1/Okp1 heterodimer to Cse4 residues 34–46 is essential for yeast growth.

evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between the loss of Ame1/Okp1 binding and cell viability upon deletion of Cse4 aa 34–46.

claim: The Mif2 signature motif and Ame1/Okp1 recognize distinct motifs at the Cse4 C- and N-terminus, respectively, and both are essential for viability.
source: The Mif2 signature motif (Xiao et al., 2017) and Ame1/Okp1 recognize distinct motifs at the Cse4 C- and N-terminus (Figure 1C), respectively, and both are essential for viability (Hornung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the XLMS data in Figure 1C and citations to prior research (Xiao et al., 2017; Hornung et al., 2014).

claim: Crosslink-derived restraints narrowed down the putative Cse4 binding site in Okp1 to amino acids 95–202.
source: To characterize the Cse4 binding site in Okp1 we applied crosslink-derived restraints to narrow down the putative interface to amino acids 95–202 of Okp1 (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the XLMS data presented in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: This region harbors a conserved stretch (aa 127–184), including part of the previously described Okp1 core domain (aa 166–211) which is essential for cell growth and whose function is still elusive.
source: Based on MSA analysis of Okp1 sequences, this region harbors a conserved stretch (aa 127–184), including part of the previously described Okp1 core domain (aa 166–211) which is essential for cell growth and whose function is still elusive (Schmitzberger et al., 2017) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on MSA analysis shown in Figure 3A and is consistent with prior research (Schmitzberger et al., 2017).

claim: Ame1/Okp1Δ123–147 bound to Cse4-NCPs as well as did the wild-type Ame1/Okp1 complex.
source: In EMSAs Ame1/Okp1Δ123–147 bound to Cse4-NCPs as well as did the wild-type Ame1/Okp1 complex, whereas Ame1/Okp1Δ140–170 associated only weakly and Ame1/Okp1Δ163–187 failed to associate with Cse4-NCPs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ame1/Okp1Δ140–170 associated only weakly with Cse4-NCPs.
source: In EMSAs Ame1/Okp1Δ123–147 bound to Cse4-NCPs as well as did the wild-type Ame1/Okp1 complex, whereas Ame1/Okp1Δ140–170 associated only weakly and Ame1/Okp1Δ163–187 failed to associate with Cse4-NCPs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ame1/Okp1Δ163–187 failed to associate with Cse4-NCPs.
source: In EMSAs Ame1/Okp1Δ123–147 bound to Cse4-NCPs as well as did the wild-type Ame1/Okp1 complex, whereas Ame1/Okp1Δ140–170 associated only weakly and Ame1/Okp1Δ163–187 failed to associate with Cse4-NCPs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Analysis of the Okp1 deletion mutants Δ123–147 and Δ163–187 in cell viability assays showed a tight correlation between their requirement for the interaction with Cse4 and being essential for yeast growth.
source: In addition, analysis of the Okp1 deletion mutants Δ123–147 and Δ163–187 in cell viability assays showed a tight correlation between their requirement for the interaction with Cse4 and being essential for yeast growth (Figure 3C) (Schmitzberger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast viability assay data shown in Figure 3C and is consistent with prior research (Schmitzberger et al., 2017).

claim: The recognition of the Cse4 nucleosome by Ame1/Okp1 is essential in budding yeast.
source: This finding further supports the notion that the recognition of the Cse4 nucleosome by Ame1/Okp1 is essential in budding yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between Okp1 mutants that cannot bind Cse4 and loss of cell viability.

claim: The COMA complex is composed of two essential, Ame1/Okp1, and two non-essential, Ctf19/Mcm21, subunits.
source: The COMA complex is composed of two essential, Ame1/Okp1, and two non-essential, Ctf19/Mcm21, subunits (Ortiz et al., 1999; Cheeseman et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Ortiz et al., 1999; Cheeseman et al., 2002).

claim: Both, Ctf19 and Mcm21 contain C-terminal tandem-RWD domains forming a rigid heterodimeric Y-shaped scaffold whose respective N-terminal RWDs of the tandems pack together as shown by a crystal structure of the K. lactis complex.
source: Both, Ctf19 and Mcm21 contain C-terminal tandem-RWD (RING finger and WD repeat containing proteins and DEAD-like helicases) domains forming a rigid heterodimeric Y-shaped scaffold whose respective N-terminal RWDs of the tandems pack together as shown by a crystal structure of the K. lactis complex (Schmitzberger and Harrison, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Schmitzberger and Harrison, 2012).

claim: The ctf19Δ or mcm21Δ mutants become synthetically lethal in a sli15ΔN background.
source: The ctf19Δ or mcm21Δ mutants become synthetically lethal in a sli15ΔN background (Campbell and Desai, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Campbell and Desai, 2013).

claim: Ame1 has been suggested to have a role in Sli15 localization close to kinetochores independently of Bir1.
source: Furthermore, Ame1 has been suggested to have a role in Sli15 localization close to kinetochores independently of Bir1 (Knockleby and Vogel, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Knockleby and Vogel, 2009).

claim: In vitro reconstitution and XLMS analysis detected 98 inter-protein and 69 intra-protein crosslinks in the Sli15/Ipl1:COMA complex.
source: To investigate whether Sli15/Ipl1 associates with the COMA complex, in vitro reconstitution and XLMS analysis detected 98 inter-protein and 69 intra-protein crosslinks (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the XLMS data presented in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: There were 10 crosslinks from the C-terminal RWD (RWD-C) domain of Ctf19 and 4 crosslinks from the Mcm21 RWD-C domain to the microtubule binding domain of Sli15 (aa 229–565).
source: In particular, there were 10 crosslinks from the C-terminal RWD (RWD-C) domain of Ctf19 and 4 crosslinks from the Mcm21 RWD-C domain to the microtubule binding domain of Sli15 (aa 229–565) (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 2, 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the XLMS data presented in Figure 4A and Supplementary files 2 and 3.

claim: In the Ame1/Okp1 heterodimer, crosslinks were identified from Sli15 to Okp1 and from Ipl1 to Ame1.
source: In the Ame1/Okp1 heterodimer, we identified crosslinks from Sli15 to Okp1 and from Ipl1 to Ame1.
evidence: This claim is based on the XLMS data presented in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The crosslink detected to lysine 366 of Okp1 is located near the identified Ctf19/Mcm21 binding site within Okp1 ('segment 1' aa 321–329).
source: The crosslink detected to lysine 366 of Okp1 is located near the identified Ctf19/Mcm21 binding site within Okp1 ('segment 1' aa 321–329) (Schmitzberger et al., 2017) and thus is close to the RWD-C domains of Ctf19 and Mcm21.
evidence: This is an inference based on the XLMS data and comparison with prior research (Schmitzberger et al., 2017).

claim: Ame1/Okp1 and Ctf19/Mcm21 were both pulled down with Sli15/Ipl1 either as individual complexes or in combination.
source: Sli15-2xStrep/Ipl1 was immobilized on Streptavidin beads and incubated with a 2-fold molar excess of either Ame1/Okp1 and Ctf19/Mcm21 using wild-type Ctf19 protein or a C-terminal deletion mutant Ctf19Δ270–369 (Ctf19ΔC). Ame1/Okp1 and Ctf19/Mcm21 were both pulled down with Sli15/Ipl1 either as individual complexes or in combination (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Recombinant Ctf19ΔC formed a stoichiometric complex with Mcm21, but lost its ability to bind Sli15/Ipl1.
source: In agreement with previous findings (Schmitzberger et al., 2017), recombinant Ctf19ΔC formed a stoichiometric complex with Mcm21, but lost its ability to bind Sli15/Ipl1 indicating that the RWD-C of Ctf19 is required for Sli15/Ipl1 interaction in vitro (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4C and is consistent with prior research (Schmitzberger et al., 2017).

claim: The RWD-C of Ctf19 is required for Sli15/Ipl1 interaction in vitro.
source: In agreement with previous findings (Schmitzberger et al., 2017), recombinant Ctf19ΔC formed a stoichiometric complex with Mcm21, but lost its ability to bind Sli15/Ipl1 indicating that the RWD-C of Ctf19 is required for Sli15/Ipl1 interaction in vitro (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Ctf19ΔC cannot bind Sli15/Ipl1.

claim: Autophosphorylation of Sli15/Ipl1 abrogated its interaction with Ame1/Okp1 and Ctf19/Mcm21.
source: Autophosphorylation of Sli15/Ipl1 abrogated its interaction with Ame1/Okp1 and Ctf19/Mcm21 indicating that like the phosphorylation-regulated binding to microtubules, phosphorylation of Sli15 by Ipl1 may prevent and regulate its binding to the COMA complex (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Phosphorylation of Sli15 by Ipl1 may prevent and regulate its binding to the COMA complex.
source: Autophosphorylation of Sli15/Ipl1 abrogated its interaction with Ame1/Okp1 and Ctf19/Mcm21 indicating that like the phosphorylation-regulated binding to microtubules, phosphorylation of Sli15 by Ipl1 may prevent and regulate its binding to the COMA complex (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that autophosphorylation of Sli15/Ipl1 abrogated its interaction with COMA.

claim: Crosslink-derived restraints identified the Ctf19 RWD-C domain as a Sli15/Ipl1 docking site within the COMA complex.
source: In summary, crosslink-derived restraints identified the Ctf19 RWD-C domain as a Sli15/Ipl1 docking site within the COMA complex, a conclusion supported by the loss of interaction upon deletion of the Ctf19 C-terminus in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by the XLMS data in Figure 4A and the in vitro binding assay data in Figure 4C.

claim: In the presence of Ctf19-FRB, cells expressing Sli15ΔN are viable, but display synthetic lethality on rapamycin containing medium.
source: First, we reproduced the reported synthetic lethality by anchoring-away Ctf19-FRB in a yeast strain, in which the endogenous SLI15 copy was replaced by sli15ΔN (Haruki et al., 2008). We found that in the presence of Ctf19-FRB, cells expressing Sli15ΔN are viable, but display synthetic lethality on rapamycin containing medium, consistent with previous findings (Campbell and Desai, 2013) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast viability assay data shown in Figure 5A and is consistent with prior research (Campbell and Desai, 2013).

claim: Cells expressing Ctf19ΔN2-30 in the sli15ΔN background were just as viable upon depletion of Ctf19-FRB as those expressing intact Ctf19.
source: Cells expressing Ctf19ΔN2-30 in the sli15ΔN background were just as viable upon depletion of Ctf19-FRB as those expressing intact Ctf19 (Figure 5A), demonstrating that the synthetic lethality is independent of the Ctf19 N-terminus and its role in cohesin loading.
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast viability assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The synthetic lethality is independent of the Ctf19 N-terminus and its role in cohesin loading.
source: Cells expressing Ctf19ΔN2-30 in the sli15ΔN background were just as viable upon depletion of Ctf19-FRB as those expressing intact Ctf19 (Figure 5A), demonstrating that the synthetic lethality is independent of the Ctf19 N-terminus and its role in cohesin loading.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Ctf19ΔN2-30 does not cause synthetic lethality with sli15ΔN.

claim: Ectopic expression of Sli15ΔN fusions to the outer kinetochore subunits Mtw1 or Dsn1 and to the inner kinetochore subunits Mif2, Ctf3 or Cnn1 did not rescue viability.
source: Ectopic expression of Sli15ΔN fusions to the outer kinetochore subunits Mtw1 or Dsn1 and to the inner kinetochore subunits Mif2, Ctf3 or Cnn1 did not rescue viability (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast viability assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Selectively tethering Sli15ΔN to Ame1 or Okp1 restored growth.
source: But selectively tethering Sli15ΔN to Ame1 or Okp1 restored growth (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast viability assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cells ectopically expressing the Sli15∆N mutant protein grew like wild-type, but displayed sensitivity to 15 µg/ml benomyl.
source: Cells ectopically expressing the Sli15∆N mutant protein grew like wild-type, but displayed sensitivity to 15 µg/ml benomyl which contrasted the previous observation that cells carrying the endogenous sli15ΔN allele were not sensitive to 12.5 µg/ml benomyl (Campbell and Desai, 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on the yeast viability assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Expression of Ame1- or Okp1-Sli15∆N∆SAH proteins rescued cell growth in the sli15ΔN background upon Ctf19 depletion.
source: While expression of Ame1- or Okp1-Sli15∆N∆SAH proteins rescued cell growth in the sli15ΔN background upon Ctf19 depletion, Ame1- and Okp1-Sli15∆N∆IN fusions did not, indicating that Ipl1 kinase activity is required (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast viability assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Ame1- and Okp1-Sli15∆N∆IN fusions did not rescue cell growth in the sli15ΔN background upon Ctf19 depletion, indicating that Ipl1 kinase activity is required.
source: While expression of Ame1- or Okp1-Sli15∆N∆SAH proteins rescued cell growth in the sli15ΔN background upon Ctf19 depletion, Ame1- and Okp1-Sli15∆N∆IN fusions did not, indicating that Ipl1 kinase activity is required (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deletion of the IN-box (Ipl1-binding domain) prevents rescue of synthetic lethality.

claim: Tethering Ipl1 activity to COMA subunits is crucial.
source: Since the ectopically expressed fusion proteins were tested in the sli15ΔN background, the result indicates that Ipl1 activity associated with endogenous Sli15ΔN could not rescue synthetic lethality and that tethering Ipl1 activity to COMA subunits is crucial.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Ame1/Okp1-Sli15ΔN fusions lacking the IN-box do not rescue synthetic lethality.

claim: Deletion of the SAH domain in Ame1- and Okp1-Sli15∆N∆SAH fusions was not lethal and was presumably rescued by the SAH domain of the endogenous Sli15ΔN protein.
source: In contrast, deletion of the SAH domain in Ame1- and Okp1-Sli15∆N∆SAH fusions was not lethal and was presumably rescued by the SAH domain of the endogenous Sli15ΔN protein (Figure 5D) suggesting that the SAH domain is not required for the function of the inner kinetochore-localized CPC pool.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that deletion of the SAH domain does not prevent rescue of synthetic lethality.

claim: The SAH domain is not required for the function of the inner kinetochore-localized CPC pool.
source: In contrast, deletion of the SAH domain in Ame1- and Okp1-Sli15∆N∆SAH fusions was not lethal and was presumably rescued by the SAH domain of the endogenous Sli15ΔN protein (Figure 5D) suggesting that the SAH domain is not required for the function of the inner kinetochore-localized CPC pool.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deletion of the SAH domain in the fusion proteins does not prevent rescue of synthetic lethality.

claim: The Ctf19 C-terminus is involved in formation of the COMA complex through binding to Okp1.
source: As recently described, the Ctf19 C-terminus is involved in formation of the COMA complex through binding to Okp1 (Schmitzberger et al., 2017) and consequently, its deletion abrogates kinetochore localization of Ctf19 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Schmitzberger et al., 2017) and microscopy data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of the Ctf19 C-terminus abrogates kinetochore localization of Ctf19.
source: As recently described, the Ctf19 C-terminus is involved in formation of the COMA complex through binding to Okp1 (Schmitzberger et al., 2017) and consequently, its deletion abrogates kinetochore localization of Ctf19 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fusions to both, the N- or C-terminus, of wild-type Ctf19 restored viability.
source: To circumvent loss of Ctf19 from kinetochores, we tested whether Ame1 or Okp1 fusions to wild-type Ctf19 or Ctf19∆C were able to rescue synthetic lethality in the sli15ΔN/CTF19-FRB background. Fusions to both, the N- or C-terminus, of wild-type Ctf19 restored viability, whereas fusions to Ctf19∆C resulted in synthetic lethality (Figure 6A) suggesting that recruitment of Ipl1 activity to the inner kinetochore mediated by the Ctf19 C-terminus is important for CPC function.
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast viability assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Fusions to Ctf19∆C resulted in synthetic lethality.
source: To circumvent loss of Ctf19 from kinetochores, we tested whether Ame1 or Okp1 fusions to wild-type Ctf19 or Ctf19∆C were able to rescue synthetic lethality in the sli15ΔN/CTF19-FRB background. Fusions to both, the N- or C-terminus, of wild-type Ctf19 restored viability, whereas fusions to Ctf19∆C resulted in synthetic lethality (Figure 6A) suggesting that recruitment of Ipl1 activity to the inner kinetochore mediated by the Ctf19 C-terminus is important for CPC function.
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast viability assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Recruitment of Ipl1 activity to the inner kinetochore mediated by the Ctf19 C-terminus is important for CPC function.
source: To circumvent loss of Ctf19 from kinetochores, we tested whether Ame1 or Okp1 fusions to wild-type Ctf19 or Ctf19∆C were able to rescue synthetic lethality in the sli15ΔN/CTF19-FRB background. Fusions to both, the N- or C-terminus, of wild-type Ctf19 restored viability, whereas fusions to Ctf19∆C resulted in synthetic lethality (Figure 6A) suggesting that recruitment of Ipl1 activity to the inner kinetochore mediated by the Ctf19 C-terminus is important for CPC function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fusions to Ctf19∆C do not rescue synthetic lethality.

claim: Depletion of Ctf19 from the nucleus resulted in a severe chromosome segregation defect.
source: Depletion of Ctf19 from the nucleus resulted in a severe chromosome segregation defect that was not observed by growing cells on medium lacking rapamycin which showed 4% red/sectored colonies (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the minichromosome loss assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Ectopic expression of the Ctf19 wild-type protein decreased the segregation defect to 19% red/sectored colonies.
source: Ectopic expression of the Ctf19 wild-type protein decreased the segregation defect to 19% red/sectored colonies (Figure 6B, Figure 6B—source data 1) and fusion of Okp1 to the C-terminus of wild-type Ctf19 reduced the red/sectored colonies to 32%.
evidence: This claim is supported by the minichromosome loss assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Fusion of Okp1 to the C-terminus of wild-type Ctf19 reduced the red/sectored colonies to 32%.
source: Ectopic expression of the Ctf19 wild-type protein decreased the segregation defect to 19% red/sectored colonies (Figure 6B, Figure 6B—source data 1) and fusion of Okp1 to the C-terminus of wild-type Ctf19 reduced the red/sectored colonies to 32%.
evidence: This claim is supported by the minichromosome loss assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The fusion of Okp1 to the Ctf19 N-terminus (Okp1-Ctf19 and Okp1-Ctf19∆C) did not rescue the segregation defect.
source: But the fusion of Okp1 to the Ctf19 N-terminus (Okp1-Ctf19 and Okp1-Ctf19∆C) did not rescue the segregation defect (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Figure 6B—source data 1), indicating that the function of the Ctf19 N-terminus is compromised by fusing it to Okp1 (Figure 6B, Figure 6B—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the minichromosome loss assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The function of the Ctf19 N-terminus is compromised by fusing it to Okp1.
source: But the fusion of Okp1 to the Ctf19 N-terminus (Okp1-Ctf19 and Okp1-Ctf19∆C) did not rescue the segregation defect (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Figure 6B—source data 1), indicating that the function of the Ctf19 N-terminus is compromised by fusing it to Okp1 (Figure 6B, Figure 6B—source data 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Okp1-Ctf19 fusions do not rescue the segregation defect.

claim: The Ctf19-Okp1 fusion rescued the segregation defect, albeit to a slightly lesser extent than the Ctf19 wild-type protein.
source: Thus, the Ctf19-Okp1 fusion rescued the segregation defect, albeit to a slightly lesser extent than the Ctf19 wild-type protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the minichromosome loss assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Ctf19∆C-Okp1, which was localized at the kinetochore, was unable to rescue the segregation defect.
source: In contrast, Ctf19∆C-Okp1, which was localized at the kinetochore (Figure 6C), was unable to rescue the segregation defect (Figure 6B, Figure 6B—source data 1) suggesting that the Ctf19 C-terminus has a role in mediating accurate chromosome segregation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the minichromosome loss assay data shown in Figure 6B and microscopy data in Figure 6C.

claim: The Ctf19 C-terminus has a role in mediating accurate chromosome segregation.
source: In contrast, Ctf19∆C-Okp1, which was localized at the kinetochore (Figure 6C), was unable to rescue the segregation defect (Figure 6B, Figure 6B—source data 1) suggesting that the Ctf19 C-terminus has a role in mediating accurate chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Ctf19∆C-Okp1 cannot rescue the segregation defect despite being localized at the kinetochore.

claim: In addition to Mif2, the Ame1/Okp1 heterodimer of the COMA complex is a direct and selective interactor of Cse4-NCPs.
source: We investigated the subunit connectivity of the inner kinetochore assembled at budding yeast point centromeres at the domain level using in vitro reconstitution and XLMS. We found that in addition to Mif2 (Xiao et al., 2017), the Ame1/Okp1 heterodimer of the COMA complex is a direct and selective interactor of Cse4-NCPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the EMSA, SEC, and XLMS data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The conserved motifs aa 163–187 of the Okp1 core domain and aa 34–46 of the Cse4 END establish the interaction between Ame1/Okp1 and Cse4.
source: We identified the conserved motifs aa 163–187 of the Okp1 core domain (Figure 3B,C) (Schmitzberger et al., 2017) and aa 34–46 (Figure 2D,E) of the Cse4 END to establish the interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the EMSA, SEC, and yeast viability assay data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The essential function of the Cse4 N-terminus and the binding interface for Ame1/Okp1 are mediated by the same 13 amino acid motif.
source: Although, we did not address whether the Cse4 residues 34–46 are required for the Ame1/Okp1 kinetochore recruitment, the notion that the essential function of the Cse4 N-terminus and the binding interface for Ame1/Okp1 are mediated by the same 13 amino acid motif (Figure 2) suggests that Ame1/Okp1 is an essential link between centromeric nucleosomes and the outer kinetochore (Hornung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deletion of Cse4 aa 34–46 both abolishes Ame1/Okp1 binding and is lethal.

claim: Ame1/Okp1 is an essential link between centromeric nucleosomes and the outer kinetochore.
source: Although, we did not address whether the Cse4 residues 34–46 are required for the Ame1/Okp1 kinetochore recruitment, the notion that the essential function of the Cse4 N-terminus and the binding interface for Ame1/Okp1 are mediated by the same 13 amino acid motif (Figure 2) suggests that Ame1/Okp1 is an essential link between centromeric nucleosomes and the outer kinetochore (Hornung et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and is consistent with prior research (Hornung et al., 2014).

claim: Recent studies have identified the same Cse4 region to interact with Ame1/Okp1.

source: Our crosslink-derived restraints are also in good agreement with a recent cryo-electron microscopy structure of a 13-subunit budding yeast inner kinetochore complex lacking the Cse4-NCP and Mif2 (Hinshaw and Harrison, 2019) showing for instance crosslinks between the C-terminal domain of Chl4 and central regions of Ctf19 and Mcm21.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with a recent cryo-EM structure (Hinshaw and Harrison, 2019).

source: Similarly in humans, recruitment of the CENP-OPQRU complex to kinetochores requires a joint interface formed by CENP-HIKM and CENP-LN (Foltz et al., 2006; Okada et al., 2006; Pesenti et al., 2018), but loss of the complex does not affect localization of other inner kinetochore proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Foltz et al., 2006; Okada et al., 2006; Pesenti et al., 2018).

evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the CENP-OPQRU complex in humans.

claim: Knockouts of CENP-U/Q in DT40 cells are viable.
source: Differences between vertebrate and budding yeast inner kinetochores are reflected by the physiological importance of the involved proteins, as Ame1/Okp1 together with Mif2 are the essential CTF19cCCAN proteins in budding yeast, whereas knockouts of CENP-U/Q in DT40 cells are viable (Hori et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Hori et al., 2008).

claim: Ctf19 and Mcm21 become essential when centromere-targeting of the CPC is lost in a sli15ΔN mutant.
source: Although the Ctf19/Mcm21 heterodimer is not essential, ctf19∆ and mcm21∆ mutants have chromosome segregation and cohesion defects (Hyland et al., 1999; Ortiz et al., 1999; Poddar et al., 1999; Fernius and Marston, 2009; Hinshaw et al., 2017). Moreover, Ctf19 and Mcm21 become essential when centromere-targeting of the CPC is lost in a sli15ΔN mutant.
evidence: This statement is based on the synthetic lethality observed between ctf19Δ/mcm21Δ and sli15ΔN.

claim: COMA interacts directly with Sli15/Ipl1.
source: Our work showed that COMA interacts directly with Sli15/Ipl1 and identified the Ctf19 RWD-C domain as the primary docking site (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the XLMS and in vitro binding assay data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Positioning Sli15/Ipl1 proximal to Ame1/Okp1 is important in vivo.
source: Synthetic lethality upon Ctf19 or Mcm21 depletion in a sli15∆N background was rescued by fusions of Sli15∆N to COMA subunits, whereas fusions to other inner or outer kinetochore proteins did not (Figure 5B). This observation suggests that positioning Sli15/Ipl1 proximal to Ame1/Okp1 is important in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that only fusions to COMA subunits rescue synthetic lethality.

claim: The observed synthetic lethality is due to mislocalized Ipl1 kinase.
source: Because of the requirement of a functional Ipl1-binding IN-box on Sli15 for restoring viability we assume that the observed synthetic lethality is due to mislocalized Ipl1 kinase (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deletion of the IN-box prevents rescue of synthetic lethality.

claim: Tethering Sli15 to the inner kinetochore might ensure the spatial positioning of Ipl1 kinase activity towards outer kinetochore substrates, required for correcting erroneous kinetochore-microtubule attachments.
source: Tethering Sli15 to the inner kinetochore might ensure the spatial positioning of Ipl1 kinase activity towards outer kinetochore substrates (Akiyoshi et al., 2013; Foley and Kapoor, 2013; Krenn and Musacchio, 2015), required for correcting erroneous kinetochore-microtubule attachments (Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation based on the data and is consistent with prior research (Akiyoshi et al., 2013; Foley and Kapoor, 2013; Krenn and Musacchio, 2015).

claim: The SAH domain is required for binding to spindle microtubules and critical for cell survival.
source: Because the SAH domain is required for binding to spindle microtubules and critical for cell survival (Samejima et al., 2015; van der Horst et al., 2015; Fink et al., 2017), we infer that the observed rescue was mediated by the SAH domain of endogenous Sli15ΔN (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Samejima et al., 2015; van der Horst et al., 2015; Fink et al., 2017).

claim: The observed rescue of COMA-Sli15ΔN fusions lacking the SAH domain was mediated by the SAH domain of endogenous Sli15ΔN.
source: Because the SAH domain is required for binding to spindle microtubules and critical for cell survival (Samejima et al., 2015; van der Horst et al., 2015; Fink et al., 2017), we infer that the observed rescue was mediated by the SAH domain of endogenous Sli15ΔN (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that COMA-Sli15ΔNΔSAH fusions rescue synthetic lethality despite lacking the SAH domain.

claim: Deletion of the Ctf19 RWD-C domain was sufficient to cause synthetic lethality with Sli15ΔN.

evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast viability assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Deletion of the Ctf19 N-terminus did not cause a synthetic effect in sli15ΔN mutant cells.
source: Moreover, assessing the initially proposed model for the synthetic growth defect of Ctf19/Mcm21 deletion in a sli15ΔN background (Campbell and Desai, 2013), we observed that deletion of the Ctf19 N-terminus did not cause a synthetic effect in sli15ΔN mutant cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the yeast viability assay data shown in Figure 5A.

evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deletion of the Ctf19 N-terminus does not cause synthetic lethality with sli15ΔN.
